usage: Can I get a menu, please
The single most useful sentence when you sit down
What staff say when handing it over
Staff saying an item isn't listed
You see the menu by QR code
Many places now have no paper menu, just a QR sticker
examples: Excuse me, could you bring the menu again?
Polite re-request once you've already ordered drinks
메뉴판이 한국어밖에 없어서 사진 보고 시켰어요.
The menu was only in Korean, so I ordered by looking at the photos.
요즘은 메뉴판 대신 테이블에서 QR로 주문해요.
These days you order by QR at the table instead of a menu.
nuance: 메뉴 means the menu in the abstract (the offerings), while 메뉴판 is the physical thing you hold or the board on the wall. When you want them to physically bring it, always say 메뉴판, not 메뉴. It's neutral/everyday register; '메뉴판 주세요' is perfectly polite in any restaurant.
mistakes: Saying '메뉴 주세요' when you mean the physical booklet — staff may think you're naming a dish; say '메뉴판 주세요'
Pronouncing it 'menu-pan' separately — it's one word, 메뉴판

usage: Polite phrasing staff use when approaching
Confirmation that the kitchen received it
Useful if you change your mind quickly
examples: 주문 아직 안 했어요. 조금만 더 볼게요.
We haven't ordered yet. We'll look a bit more.
Buying time when staff come too early
If you order by kiosk, it's card only.
Since it's a big group, the order all went in at once.
nuance: 주문 is the noun (the order); the verb is 주문하다, already common. Knowing the bare noun lets you understand staff phrases like '주문 도와드릴게요' and '주문 들어갔어요', which you hear constantly. Neutral register, used identically in casual and formal dining.
mistakes: Confusing 주문 (food order) with 주말 (weekend) — different words
Using 시키다 only — 주문하다 sounds slightly more polite/standard when talking to staff

english: an extra order / addition (more of something)
usage: An extra bowl of rice, please
'추가요' alone works as a full request
Asking if extra noodles are available
Calling staff for a second round
Checking if the add-on costs more
examples: We finished the meat, so we added two more portions.
Side dishes are free even if you ask for more.
Important cultural point about 반찬 refills
Adding cheese to the ramen is 1,000 won.
nuance: 추가 covers any add-on: more rice, more meat, an extra topping, a second drink. Attaching -요 ('추가요') turns it into a complete spoken request, which is how locals order more without a full sentence. It's casual-but-polite and works everywhere. The verb form is 추가하다.
mistakes: Saying '더 주세요' for paid add-ons — fine for free 반찬, but for paid items say 'X 추가요' so staff ring it up
Forgetting that '추가' may cost money — always confirm with '추가 요금 있어요?'

usage: The key question — confirms it's free
Common at salad bars / certain cafes
examples: Can I refill the cola here?
Most fast-food and some restaurants offer free soda refills
You can refill side dishes at the self-serve corner.
The coffee refill is free only once.
nuance: 리필 (from English 'refill') specifically implies getting more of the same thing for free, unlike 추가, which often costs money. Use it for drinks, side dishes, or coffee. Casual register; '리필 돼요?' is the natural way to check the policy before assuming.
mistakes: Assuming all refills are free — always ask '리필 돼요?' first; some places charge
Mixing up 리필 (free same-item top-up) with 추가 (extra, often paid)

english: pager / buzzer (that vibrates when food is ready)
usage: Come when the buzzer goes off
What's expected after you pick up food
Where do I get the buzzer?
examples: The buzzer went off, so I went to get the food.
주문하면 진동벨 주는데 울리면 직접 가져와야 해요.
When you order they give a buzzer, and when it rings you pick it up yourself.
The buzzer vibrates and lights up together.
nuance: 진동벨 (literally 'vibration bell') is the pager you're handed at counter-service spots, food courts, and many cafes. Recognizing the word matters because staff will say '진동벨 울리면 오세요' and expect you to fetch the food yourself. Everyday neutral register.
mistakes: Waiting at the table expecting table service after getting a 진동벨 — you must go pick up the food yourself
Walking off with the 진동벨 — remember '반납' (return it) at the counter

usage: Where you grab water, side dishes, utensils
Staff pointing you to the station
examples: Water and pickled radish are self-serve. Get them over there.
여기 셀프라서 수저도 직접 챙겨야 해요.
It's self-serve here, so you grab your own utensils too.
Coffee refills are free at the self-serve corner.
nuance: 셀프 (from 'self') tells you no one will bring it — water, utensils, side dishes, or refills are yours to fetch. When you see '셀프' on a sign or hear '물은 셀프예요', stand up and get it. Casual everyday register, ubiquitous in Korean eateries.
mistakes: Waiting for staff to bring water when a sign says '물 셀프' — get it yourself from the dispenser
Reading it as a brand name — 셀프 just means self-service here

usage: Make it a large (double) portion, please
How much is the large portion?
examples: I was starving, so I ordered the large jjamppong.
Very natural use at a Chinese restaurant
곱빼기는 보통 천 원 더 받아요.
A large portion usually costs 1,000 won more.
Even though I got the large, it wasn't enough.
nuance: 곱빼기 means roughly a double serving and is mostly used for noodle and rice dishes (짜장면, 짬뽕, 볶음밥). Saying 'X 곱빼기로 주세요' is the local way to get more food for a small surcharge. Casual register; you'll mainly hear it at Chinese-Korean and noodle spots.
mistakes: Using 곱빼기 for soups or BBQ — it's tied to noodle/rice bowls; for meat use '추가' or '2인분'
Saying '큰 거 주세요' — understandable, but '곱빼기로 주세요' is what locals actually say

usage: The set is cheaper than à la carte
examples: I'll get the burger as a combo, not just the burger alone.
단품 vs 세트 contrast, very common
세트로 시키면 음료랑 감자튀김이 같이 나와요.
If you order the set, a drink and fries come with it.
The chicken is sold as a set bundled with cola.
nuance: 세트 (from 'set') is a combo — a main plus drink and/or sides at a bundled price, the opposite of 단품 (à la carte). Asking for '세트로 주세요' is the default at fast food and many casual spots. Neutral everyday register.
mistakes: Assuming the displayed price is the 세트 price — it's often the 단품 price; ask '세트로 얼마예요?'
Confusing 세트 (combo) with 사이드 (the side item itself)

english: a side dish / side item (menu add-on)
usage: What side items do you have?
I'll have fries as a side
The main and a side together
examples: While ordering chicken, I added cheese balls as a side.
The side items are pricier than I expected.
For pizza sides I ordered cola and wings.
nuance: 사이드 (from 'side') means the optional side items on a menu — fries, wings, cheese balls — distinct from the free Korean 반찬. You'll see a '사이드 메뉴' section especially at chicken, pizza, and burger places. Casual register, heavily used in delivery ordering.
mistakes: Confusing 사이드 (a paid menu side) with 반찬 (free Korean side dishes)
Expecting 사이드 to be free — these are ordered and charged separately

english: a course meal (multi-dish set served in order)
usage: Do you have a course menu?
What's the difference between course A and B?
How much is the course per person?
Course prices are usually per person
examples: It's an anniversary, so I booked a course meal.
The course is usually available for two or more people.
At omakase the chef serves a course at their discretion.
nuance: 코스 (from 'course') is a multi-dish meal served in sequence at a fixed per-person price, common for dates, anniversaries, and upscale or 오마카세 dining. Tiers are often labeled A코스/B코스. Slightly more formal context than everyday eating, but the word itself is neutral.
mistakes: Thinking the 코스 price is for the whole table — it's almost always per person (1인당)
Confusing 코스 (a set course meal) with 세트 (a fast-food-style combo)

usage: Can I make a group reservation?
Key question for booking for many people
examples: I made a group reservation for 10 for a work dinner.
For large groups, please decide on one menu in advance.
I'll show your group to the room in the back.
nuance: 단체 refers to a large group eating together — think work dinners (회식), club gatherings, or family events. Restaurants often have special rules: 단체 예약, 단체석, or a required unified menu. Neutral register; you'll use it whenever booking for roughly five or more people.
mistakes: Using 단체 for just two or three people — that's not a 단체; reserve the word for larger parties
Assuming a 단체 can always walk in — big groups usually need '단체 예약' ahead of time

usage: Basic way to order by serving
Meat is usually priced per portion
I'm alone, so just one portion
examples: Two portions of pork belly and a soybean stew, please.
Standard BBQ order; meat counted in 인분
Here you can't order one portion; it's from two.
When eating alone I felt awkward ordering just one portion.
nuance: 1인분 (一人分) is the per-person serving unit, used above all for meat at BBQ and for portioned dishes. Crucial detail: many grill places enforce a 2인분부터 (two-portion minimum), so a solo diner should check first. Read as '일인분'. Neutral everyday register.
mistakes: Pronouncing it 'one-inbun' — read the numeral in Korean: 일인분
Assuming you can always order 1인분 at BBQ — many spots require 2인분 minimum, so ask first
